scope: Published 2025–2026 source evidence only; no live agent investigation or execution of fetched code.

candidates.title: Anthropic: sixteen Claudes building a C compiler
mechanisms: human-built GCC oracle to repair decomposition
candidates.run_count_rule: One selected Opus 4.6 compiler episode, not the earlier model-series benchmarks.

what_happened_dates.text: **What happened / dates.** Nicholas Carlini’s February 5, 2026 disclosure describes sixteen Opus 4.6 agents constructing a Rust C compiler across two weeks and nearly 2,000 Claude Code sessions, at just under $20,000.[1] Exact run boundaries are not supplied.[1] Reported outputs include bootable Linux 6.9 builds on x86, ARM and RISC-V and approximately 99% pass rates on most compiler test suites.[1] This is an executed capability stress test, not a production compiler deployment.[1]

collective_relevance.text: **Collective relevance.** The meaningful phenomenon is artifact-mediated task allocation among simultaneous writers, not 100,000 lines of generated code.[1] Agents claim work, incorporate others’ commits and select subsequent tasks without an orchestration agent.[1] The revealing collective failure came at the Linux build: all sixteen encountered the same blocking bug, duplicated its repair and overwrote one another.[1] Increasing population did not help until the human changed the task’s decomposition.[1]

available_evidence.text: **Available evidence.** The primary engineering account specifies locks, containers, merges, test sampling and interventions; the public repository provides task-lock directories and commit links.[1][8] The repository’s human-authored disclaimer says the code has not been validated for correctness and that generated documentation may make false claims.[8] No independent compiler conformance or security evaluation is present in this bundle.[1][8] Build success is narrower than language correctness.[1][8]

autonomy_control_topology.text: **Autonomy / control topology.** A human specified the compiler goal and some architecture, designed and revised the verifier, introduced CI, assigned specialist roles and devised the GCC oracle.[1] Within that environment, peer agents choose the next problem, implement fixes, resolve conflicts and maintain progress notes; no high-level orchestrator is used.[1] The loop starts new sessions repeatedly, rather than one persistent agent thinking for two weeks.[1] This is decentralized task selection on centrally provided infrastructure, with substantive human feedback engineering—not “humans never intervened.”[1]

coordination_substrate.text: **Coordination substrate.** Each Docker container clones a shared bare Git repository.[1] An agent writes a task file under `current_tasks/`; Git synchronization makes a competing claimant select another task.[1] It then works, pulls and merges upstream changes, pushes and releases its lock.[1] READMEs, progress files and failed-approach notes help replacement sessions orient themselves.[1] Tests provide the action–feedback–next-action loop; deterministic per-agent subsampling reduces wasted test time.[1] Shared Git is therefore an operational coordination medium, not merely an evidentiary archive.[1]

strong_speculative_failures.text: **Strong versus speculative / failures.** Strong as an operator disclosure: agents continued work, collided on a common blocker and benefited from a human-built GCC differential oracle that split kernel files across agents; some failures still required delta-debugging pairs of files.[1] New features repeatedly regressed existing functionality.[1] Remaining limits include a GCC fallback for x86 16-bit boot code, buggy assembler/linker work, poor generated-code efficiency and failure to be a drop-in compiler.[1] Generated README claims of standalone tooling and drop-in compatibility must not override the human account or disclaimer; this bundle cannot establish that those limitations were subsequently resolved.[1][8] Neither test pass rate nor autonomous code volume demonstrates emergent intelligence.[1]

distinctness.text: **Distinctness.** A separate Anthropic engineering episode from the excluded August 13 emerging-multiagent experiments; a compiler-construction workload, not the excluded exfiltration, wiki-collusion or PixelLeak families.[1] Distinct from Cursor in operator, model, activity episode and topology: peer task locks plus a human-engineered oracle, versus recursive planning and assigned workers.[1][2] Earlier Claude compiler benchmarks mentioned in the same disclosure are not additional cases.[1]

candidates.title: Cursor: FastRender’s long-running many-agent browser experiment
candidates.evidence_class: executed provider research project with independent limited artifact check
candidates.run_count_rule: One FastRender case across multiple reports; do not add the other artifacts enumerated in Cursor post.

what_happened_dates.text: **What happened / dates.** Cursor disclosed the experiment on January 14, 2026; Wilson Lin’s January 23 interview adds operational detail.[2][3] FastRender originated as his November 2025 side project before becoming a Cursor research project.[3] The January disclosure reports a browser run of close to a week; the interview places the longest uninterrupted autonomous run at about one week, within a research program of about three weeks.[2][3] Do not turn the program duration into one continuous run.[3]

collective_relevance.text: **Collective relevance.** The project documents a transition from flat self-coordination to hierarchical task generation, together with failure modes of both.[2] Initially, agents claimed work through a shared file and locks: forgotten or long-held locks reduced twenty agents to the effective throughput of two or three.[2] Optimistic concurrency helped mechanics but not risk aversion: agents made safe small changes while no one owned hard end-to-end problems.[2] These are actual reported collective pathologies, not merely a large repository.[2]

available_evidence.text: **Available evidence.** Cursor’s account provides the architecture and public artifact link.[2] The published Lin interview includes a harness demo, precise mechanisms and concessions.[3] Approximately 2,000 concurrent agents at the peak is Lin’s later operator report; January 14 described hundreds, and the figures must not be added or treated as independently verified counts.[2][3] Simon Willison independently followed build instructions and obtained a working browser window with recognizable Google and blog pages, but visible rendering glitches.[4] Fortune interviewed Cursor and OpenAI personnel and reported that the system remained incomplete and nonproduction-ready.[5]

autonomy_control_topology.text: **Autonomy / control topology.** Planners continually inspect the codebase and create tasks, recursively spawning sub-planners; workers complete assigned tasks and push changes without coordinating directly with other workers.[2] A judge decides whether another cycle should run, followed by fresh starts.[2] Humans designed prompts, selected models and divided browser workstreams across harnesses.[2][3] Lin says they could stop a running execution but did not steer its trajectory.[3] This is substantial ongoing model decision authority inside an engineered hierarchy, not a flat decentralized swarm.[2][3]

coordination_substrate.text: **Coordination substrate.** Planner task trees and the shared Git branch mediate work allocation and integration.[2][3] Scope partitioning and modular code reportedly minimize overlapping edits; an integrator role was removed because it bottlenecked work.[2][3] Specification submodules, Rust compilation and screenshot comparison against golden samples supply grounding and feedback.[3] Screenshots are part of the disclosed feedback design, not an independent guarantee of browser correctness.[3] Multiple harnesses on separate large machines handled workstreams such as CSS; Lin described roughly 300 concurrent agents per machine.[3]

strong_speculative_failures.text: **Strong versus speculative / failures.** Strongest result: a coordinated autonomous run produced an artifact that an independent developer could build and use for limited page rendering.[2][4] Initial public CI failed and build instructions were missing; later instructions enabled Willison’s build.[4] JavaScript was not working in the January 23 demo and agents had disabled it behind a feature flag.[3] They autonomously chose dependencies—including Taffy and a QuickJS workaround to unblock work while other agents built the JavaScript engine—complicating “from scratch.” Lin explicitly allowed transient compilation/API errors to avoid synchronization bottlenecks; his claim that errors stayed at a stable rate is not independently measured here.[3] Cursor still required fresh starts against drift, and Lin said production software was never the goal.[2][3] Repo size, commit rate and a screenshot establish neither completeness nor correctness.[2][3][4]

distinctness.text: **Distinctness.** Separate operator and episode from Anthropic’s compiler and all excluded seed families.[1][2] The January disclosure, January 19 build check and January 23 interview describe the same browser project, not three swarms.[2][3][4] Its Solid-to-React migration, video-rendering improvement, Java LSP, emulator and spreadsheet listings are not split into independent collective cases: project outcome lists alone do not establish separate comparable many-agent runs.[2]

candidates.title: Optional comparator: Cursor/NVIDIA CUDA-kernel optimization
candidates.evidence_class: executed workload-derived optimization evaluation; not documented production deployment
candidates.run_count_rule: One separately disclosed experiment family, containing two language-separated runs; no evidence of independent swarm populations for each problem.

what_happened_dates.text: **What happened / dates.** April 14, 2026 disclosure: a three-week multi-agent optimization experiment over 235 workload-derived problems evaluated on 27 Blackwell B200 GPUs.[6] Retain as an executed technical experiment, not deployed production inference infrastructure.[6] Exact activity boundaries are absent.[6]

collective_relevance.text: **Collective relevance.** A planner distributed and rebalanced autonomous workers using performance metrics.[6] The system repeatedly benchmarked, debugged and optimized kernels—clear feedback-driven coordination beyond parallel text generation.[6]

available_evidence.text: **Available evidence.** Provider collaboration account plus a public results repository listing kernel solutions, per-workload/per-problem metrics and traces.[6][7] Individual CSVs and trace bodies were not examined here; this is not an independent rerun.[7]

autonomy_control_topology.text: **Autonomy / topology.** Hierarchical planner–worker operation; the operator reports no developer intervention in the optimization loop.[6] Human-provided problems, evaluator, documentation and protocol define the environment.[6] The source says all 235 problems were addressed in a single run, but separately specifies two language-separated runs, CUDA C/inline PTX and CuTe DSL.[6] Count one experiment family; do not manufacture 235 swarms or treat the headline as clearly language-specific.[6]

coordination_substrate.text: **Substrate.** A single Markdown protocol specified output formats, rules and tests; benchmark results informed work reallocation and subsequent optimization.[6] The evaluator was designed to invalidate implausible hardware performance, including caching-based cheating.[6] Detailed scheduler telemetry and exact agent count are absent.[6]

strong_speculative_failures.text: **Strong versus speculative / failures.** Reported 1.38× geometric-mean speedup is versus single-agent-optimized PyTorch, not uniformly best human libraries.[6] Only 149/235 problems outperformed baselines; median SOL score was 0.56, and an illustrated GEMM reached 86% of cuBLAS performance.[6] One attention-kernel substitution reportedly improved SGLang time-to-first-token by 3%—a bounded integration test, not fleet-wide adoption.[6] Universal expert superiority, causal benefits of coordination and scaling gains from more GPUs remain unestablished.[6]

distinctness.text: **Distinctness.** Same Cursor harness lineage, but a later, explicitly separate NVIDIA workload/optimization episode rather than another outcome from the browser post.[6] Mechanism and measurement are useful comparators; lower priority because the setting remains evaluation-heavy and its independent agent population is not documented.[6]

deduplication: Same-browser primary post, independent build report, interview and Fortune coverage are source records, not separate cases.
Other Cursor January project outputs are not individually counted.
April kernel experiment is later distinct work, but same harness lineage; two language runs retained under one family.
excluded_seed_families: July 2026 OpenAI Artifactory/Hugging Face, including METR/SwarmTraces
